title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
description: Brute force to optimized: computing the actual (overflow-prone) factorial versus counting factors of 5 directly with Legendre's formula.

blocks.text: Given a number n, count how many trailing zeroes appear at the end of n factorial (n factorial being the product of every whole number from 1 up to n), without actually computing that enormous number.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Factory That Needs Two Kinds of Parts to Make a Zero
blocks.text: Picture a factory where producing a single trailing zero requires pairing one "2 part" with one "5 part". The factory has a huge surplus of 2 parts, since roughly every other number contributes one, but only a trickle of 5 parts, since only every fifth number contributes one. No matter how many 2 parts pile up unused, the factory can never produce more zeroes than it has 5 parts to pair them with. Counting trailing zeroes is really just counting how many 5 parts are available.

blocks.caption: A trailing zero needs both a 2 and a 5; 5s are the scarce ingredient

Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what actually creates a trailing zero.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A trailing zero in any number comes from a factor of 10, and 10 itself is just 2 multiplied by 5.

Observation 2: Among the numbers from 1 to n, factors of 2 show up roughly twice as often as factors of 5, since every even number contributes a 2, but only every fifth number contributes a 5.

Observation 3: Since factors of 2 are always in surplus, the number of complete 2-and-5 pairs, and therefore the number of trailing zeroes, is limited entirely by how many factors of 5 are available.

Observation 4: Counting factors of 5 can be done directly by counting multiples of 5, then multiples of 25 (which contribute a second factor of 5 each), then multiples of 125, and so on, all without ever computing the actual, enormous factorial value.
That reasoning alone already points past building the factorial entirely, straight at counting factors of 5.

The most literal approach is to actually compute n factorial by multiplying every number from 2 up to n together, then repeatedly divide the result by 10, counting each clean division, until a division leaves a remainder.

items: Multiply every whole number from 2 up to n together to build the full factorial.
While the result is evenly divisible by 10, divide it by 10 and increase a counter.
Stop once dividing by 10 leaves a remainder.
Return the counter.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: build the actual factorial, then strip trailing zeroes one at a time

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The factorial is built by multiplying every number from 2 up to n in a simple loop, deliberately mirroring the literal mathematical definition of n factorial with no shortcuts.

The trailing zero counting loop divides by 10 repeatedly rather than checking individual digits, since repeatedly stripping a factor of 10 is the most direct way to count how many times 10 divides evenly into a number.

This version is written to make its own failure visible: the comment on the multiplication step exists specifically to flag that this is not just slow, it silently overflows and produces wrong answers for realistic inputs.

blocks.text: This works correctly in principle, since it counts trailing zeroes exactly as the problem describes, directly from the real value of n factorial.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text: Time and space: factorial grows so fast that n factorial has roughly n times log(n) digits, meaning even the multiplication step alone becomes extremely expensive for even moderately sized n.

Limitation: this approach is not just slow, it is fundamentally broken for real inputs. n factorial overflows a standard 64-bit integer once n reaches the low 20s, meaning this code silently produces the wrong answer for most valid inputs, without any error or warning. There is no need to compute the actual giant number at all, only the count of trailing zeroes matters, and that count can be found directly from n factorial's prime factorization.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why computing the actual factorial works in theory but fails in practice: n factorial grows so explosively fast that it overflows any fixed width integer type long before n gets large, making the brute force not just slow but outright wrong for realistic inputs.

What is actually being asked for: only the count of trailing zeroes, a tiny piece of information compared to the astronomically large full factorial value itself.

Can that count be derived without ever building the full number: yes, since trailing zeroes come from pairs of factors of 2 and 5, and factors of 5 are always the scarce ingredient limiting how many pairs exist.

How can factors of 5 be counted without factoring every number individually: by counting multiples of 5 up to n, then multiples of 25, then 125, and so on, since each higher power of 5 contributes an extra factor per multiple.

The core idea: sum n divided by 5, plus n divided by 25, plus n divided by 125, and so on, until the power of 5 exceeds n.

A trailing zero comes from a factor of 10, which is a factor of 2 multiplied by a factor of 5. Among the numbers from 1 to n, factors of 2 are far more common than factors of 5 (every other number contributes a 2, but only every fifth number contributes a 5), so the number of trailing zeroes is limited entirely by how many times 5 divides into n factorial.
The optimization is to count factors of 5 directly, without ever multiplying anything together.

Count how many multiples of 5 are at most n, then how many multiples of 25 (which each contribute an extra factor of 5), then 125, and so on, adding all of these counts together. This is known as Legendre's formula.

blocks.text: 25 factorial has exactly 6 trailing zeroes, matching the well known result for this input.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: count multiples of 5, 25, 125, and so on, directly

blocks.text: This works because every multiple of 5 up to n contributes at least one factor of 5 to n factorial, every multiple of 25 contributes one additional factor beyond that, since 25 itself is 5 times 5, every multiple of 125 contributes yet another beyond that, and so on. Summing n divided by 5, plus n divided by 25, plus n divided by 125, correctly counts every factor of 5 across every number from 1 to n, without ever needing to know what n factorial's actual, enormous value is. Since factors of 2 are always more abundant than factors of 5, this total factor-of-5 count is exactly the number of complete 2-and-5 pairs, which is exactly the number of trailing zeroes.

items: power_of_five starts at 5 and is multiplied by 5 every iteration, walking through 5, 25, 125, 625, and so on, exactly the sequence of powers Legendre's formula needs to sum over.
The loop condition stops once power_of_five exceeds n, since a power of 5 larger than n cannot possibly divide evenly into any number from 1 to n, contributing nothing further to the count.
Integer division of n by power_of_five at each step counts exactly how many multiples of that specific power of 5 exist up to n, and these counts are simply added together across every power.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log base 5 of n), since each step multiplies the power of 5 by another factor of 5.
Space: O(1). This never touches the actual value of n factorial, sidestepping the overflow problem entirely, and is already effectively optimal since it must at least look at every relevant power of 5 up to n.

blocks.text: The core pattern here is recognizing that a question about a huge, impractical to compute number (n factorial) can often be answered by reasoning about its prime factorization instead, without ever constructing the number itself. Spotting that 5s are the bottleneck, not 2s, is the key insight that makes this problem tractable.

items: Attempting to compute n factorial directly for larger n, which silently overflows and produces wrong answers rather than an obvious error.
Counting factors of 2 instead of factors of 5, the opposite of the actual bottleneck.
Forgetting that numbers like 25 or 125 contribute more than one factor of 5 each, which is why powers of 5 need to be summed, not just counted once.

blocks.text: This problem is a strong test of whether a candidate reaches for prime factorization reasoning instead of brute force simulation, especially once the numbers involved are clearly too large to compute directly. Explaining why factors of 5, not 2, are the bottleneck demonstrates real number theory intuition rather than a memorized formula.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid computing the actual factorial", think: count factors of 5 directly using Legendre's formula.
If the interviewer says "why factors of 5 and not 2", think: factors of 2 are always more abundant, so factors of 5 are the true bottleneck on trailing zeroes.
If the interviewer says "what about numbers like 25 or 125", think: each contributes more than one factor of 5, which is exactly why higher powers of 5 need their own term in the sum.

items: Why does this problem's brute force approach fail even for moderately large n, beyond just being slow?
Can you explain why factors of 2 are never the limiting factor for trailing zeroes?
How would Legendre's formula change if you needed to count trailing zeroes in a different base, not base 10?
Can you compute how many times a specific prime p divides into n factorial, generalizing beyond just p = 5?
What is the largest n for which this problem's answer could still be computed using the naive brute force without overflowing a given integer type?
Legendre's formula in general, for counting how many times any prime p divides into n factorial, of which counting factors of 5 here is just one specific case.
Any problem where a question about an impractically large number can be answered by reasoning about its prime factorization instead of constructing the number itself.
Combinatorics problems involving binomial coefficients, which often reuse this exact same factor-counting idea to determine divisibility or compute results modulo a prime.
Overflow-aware problem recognition in general, spotting when a literal, direct simulation is not just slow but actually mathematically incorrect due to representational limits.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force approach is not just slow, it is incorrect for most real inputs due to integer overflow, since n factorial itself grows far too large to represent. The optimized approach based on counting factors of 5 runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space, and is both correct and efficient for any valid input.

items: Pattern: reasoning about a number's prime factorization, specifically counting factors of 5, instead of computing the number itself; Legendre's formula.

Core Idea: trailing zeroes come from pairs of factors of 2 and 5, factors of 2 are always in surplus, so the count of trailing zeroes equals the total count of factors of 5 across every number from 1 to n, found by summing n divided by 5, 25, 125, and so on.
Time: technically O(n) multiplications for the brute force, but the result itself is wrong for realistic n due to overflow; O(log base 5 of n) for the optimized formula.
Space: O(1) for the optimized formula; the brute force's factorial value conceptually needs far more space than any fixed integer type provides.

Most Important Observation: this problem's brute force is not merely inefficient, it is actually incorrect for real inputs, making the prime factorization insight not just an optimization but a correctness fix.
Interview Difficulty: easy to state the direct approach, but reaching for Legendre's formula, and explaining why 5s are the bottleneck, is what separates a working answer from a broken one.
One line memory trick: count factors of 5, the 5s, 25s, 125s, never build the actual factorial.
